summary: Zinc chloride injection is a trace-element additive used to supplement intravenous solutions during total parenteral nutrition (TPN) to maintain zinc levels and prevent deficiency. The usual adult dose is 2.5-4 mg zinc/day (an extra 2 mg/day in acute catabolic states); full-term infants and children up to 5 years receive 100 mcg/kg/day, and small premature infants up to 300 mcg/kg/day. It must be diluted (in at least 100 mL of fluid) and never given undiluted by direct IV or IM injection because of its acidic pH.
indications: Supplement to intravenous solutions during total parenteral nutrition to maintain plasma zinc and prevent deficiency
Prevention and correction of zinc deficiency in patients requiring parenteral nutrition

An additional 2 mg zinc/day above maintenance

Do NOT give undiluted by direct IM or IV injection - the acidic pH causes tissue irritation

Periodically assess zinc status and adjust the dose to maintain normal levels
moa: Zinc is an essential trace element and a cofactor for more than 70 enzymes involved in metabolism, including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, RNA and DNA polymerases. It is necessary for normal growth, wound healing, skin integrity, immune function, taste and protein and nucleic acid synthesis. Parenteral zinc chloride replaces zinc in patients whose oral/enteral intake is inadequate, preventing the clinical manifestations of deficiency.

absolute: None known to zinc chloride itself
relative: Direct undiluted IM or IV injection (contraindicated - acidic pH, tissue irritation)
Renal impairment (risk of aluminum accumulation with prolonged use)
monitor: Aluminum with prolonged administration in renal impairment

preg: Zinc requirements are increased during pregnancy. Parenteral zinc to maintain normal zinc status is appropriate when oral intake is inadequate; deficiency itself is harmful to the fetus. Use to meet, not exceed, requirements.
lact: Zinc is a normal constituent of human milk. Supplementation to maintain normal maternal zinc status during parenteral nutrition is considered appropriate; avoid excessive dosing.
renal: Use with caution. The product contains aluminum that may reach toxic levels with prolonged parenteral administration in patients with impaired renal function, including premature neonates; monitor accordingly. Zinc itself is excreted primarily via the gastrointestinal tract.
hepatic: Zinc is excreted in part through the bile and intestine. In significant hepatic or biliary dysfunction, monitor zinc status closely and adjust the dose, as impaired excretion may predispose to accumulation.

moderate: Copper - high or prolonged zinc supplementation reduces copper absorption/levels and can cause copper-deficiency anemia and neutropenia
Tetracycline / quinolone antibiotics - zinc can reduce their absorption (relevant to enteral, not the IV additive)
minor: Iron - large doses may compete for absorption (enteral)
Penicillamine - zinc may reduce its efficacy
interactions.food: Not applicable; administered as an IV additive to parenteral nutrition.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum zinc and copper; prolonged use may require aluminum monitoring in renal impairment.

common: Generally well tolerated at recommended doses
Local irritation if given inadequately diluted
serious: Copper deficiency with prolonged excessive zinc (sideroblastic anemia, neutropenia)
Aluminum toxicity with prolonged use in renal impairment (CNS and bone effects)
rare: Hyperzincemia from overdose (nausea, vomiting, hypotension, pulmonary edema)
emergency: Acute zinc toxicity with cardiovascular collapse (from gross overdose)
Severe aluminum toxicity in vulnerable patients

monitoring: Serum copper (risk of secondary copper deficiency)
Clinical signs of zinc deficiency (diarrhea, apathy, depression, dermatitis, poor wound healing)
Aluminum levels with prolonged administration in renal impairment
Overall trace-element and nutritional status during TPN
counsel: This is given by your care team as part of intravenous nutrition; it is not self-administered
It supplies zinc, an essential mineral your body needs when you cannot eat normally
Tell your team about kidney problems - the product contains aluminum that can build up
Report poor wound healing, skin rash, hair loss, taste changes, diarrhea or low mood (signs of imbalance)
Long-term use is monitored with blood tests for zinc and copper
pk: Immediate availability (IV); incorporated into zinc-dependent enzymes
Distributes rapidly to tissues after infusion
pearls: IV trace-element additive - must be diluted (at least 100 mL); never give undiluted by direct IV/IM push (acidic pH)
Standard adult maintenance is 2.5-4 mg zinc/day; add 2 mg/day in acute catabolic states; replace large GI losses generously
Pediatric dosing is weight-based: 100 mcg/kg/day (term/children <=5 y), up to 300 mcg/kg/day in small premature infants
Prolonged high-dose zinc induces copper deficiency - monitor copper
Aluminum content can accumulate in renal impairment and neonates with prolonged use
missed: Not applicable for patient self-administration. Zinc chloride is added to parenteral nutrition by the clinical team; if a daily TPN trace-element dose is omitted, it is corrected by the prescribing/pharmacy team in subsequent bags rather than doubled.
overdose: Acute zinc overdose can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, dehydration and, with massive exposure, pulmonary edema and cardiovascular collapse. Prolonged excess causes copper deficiency (anemia, neutropenia). Treatment is to stop zinc, provide supportive care, correct fluids/electrolytes, and use chelation (e.g., calcium EDTA) for severe poisoning.
